name: Apple___Apple_scab
cause: Caused by the fungus Venturia inaequalis. Thrives in cool, wet spring weather when spores are released from infected leaf litter.
symptoms: Olive-green to brown velvety spots on leaves and fruit. Infected leaves may curl and drop early. Fruit develops scabby, corky lesions.
cure: Apply fungicides (captan, myclobutanil) at bud break and repeat every 7-14 days during wet weather. Prune and destroy infected leaves and twigs.
prevention: Plant resistant apple varieties. Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn. Ensure good air circulation through proper pruning.

name: Apple___Black_rot
cause: Caused by the fungus Botryosphaeria obtusa. Enters through wounds and spreads in warm, humid conditions.
symptoms: Brown rotting spots on fruit that enlarge and turn black. Leaves show frog-eye spots with purple margins. Cankers form on branches.
cure: Prune and remove all infected wood, mummified fruit, and cankers. Apply fungicides during the growing season. Destroy all infected material.
prevention: Maintain tree vigor with proper fertilization. Remove dead wood promptly. Avoid wounding trees during pruning.

name: Apple___Cedar_apple_rust
cause: Caused by the fungus Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae. Requires both apple and juniper/cedar trees to complete its life cycle.
symptoms: Bright orange-yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces. Tube-like structures on leaf undersides. Distorted fruit with orange lesions.
cure: Apply fungicides (myclobutanil, mancozeb) from pink bud stage through 3-4 weeks after petal fall. Remove nearby juniper hosts if possible.
prevention: Plant rust-resistant apple varieties. Avoid planting apples near eastern red cedars or ornamental junipers.

name: Cherry___Powdery_mildew
cause: Caused by the fungus Podosphaera clandestina. Spreads in warm, dry days with cool, humid nights.
symptoms: White powdery coating on young leaves and shoots. Infected leaves curl and become distorted. Fruit may show russeting.
cure: Apply sulfur-based fungicides or potassium bicarbonate sprays. Remove and destroy heavily infected shoots.
prevention: Ensure good air circulation. Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization. Plant resistant varieties.

name: Corn___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray_leaf_spot
cause: Caused by the fungus Cercospora zeae-maydis. Favored by warm, humid conditions and minimum tillage practices.
symptoms: Rectangular, tan to gray lesions with distinct parallel edges running between leaf veins. Lesions may coalesce causing large dead areas.
cure: Apply foliar fungicides (strobilurins, triazoles) at early disease onset. Use resistant hybrids.
prevention: Rotate crops, till infected residue, and plant resistant hybrids.

name: Corn___Common_rust
cause: Caused by the fungus Puccinia sorghi. Spores are wind-blown from southern regions each season.
symptoms: Small, oval to elongated, brick-red to brown pustules scattered on both leaf surfaces. Pustules turn dark brown-black late in season.
cure: Apply fungicides (triazoles, strobilurins) if disease appears before tasseling on susceptible hybrids.
prevention: Plant resistant corn hybrids. Early planting can help avoid peak spore periods.

name: Corn___Northern_Leaf_Blight
cause: Caused by the fungus Exserohilum turcicum. Favored by moderate temperatures and high humidity.
symptoms: Long, elliptical, grayish-green to tan lesions (1-6 inches) on leaves. Lesions may have wavy margins and dark borders.
cure: Apply fungicides at early tassel stage. Use resistant hybrids for future plantings.
prevention: Crop rotation, residue management, and planting resistant hybrids.

name: Grape___Black_rot
cause: Caused by the fungus Guignardia bidwellii. Spreads rapidly in warm, wet weather during the growing season.
symptoms: Circular tan spots with dark borders on leaves. Infected berries shrivel into hard, black mummies. Dark lesions on shoots.
cure: Apply fungicides (mancozeb, myclobutanil) from bud break through veraison. Remove and destroy mummified fruit.
prevention: Remove all mummified berries and infected canes during dormant pruning. Ensure good canopy airflow.

name: Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles)
cause: Caused by a fungal complex including Phaeomoniella chlamydospora and Phaeoacremonium spp. Enters through pruning wounds.
symptoms: Tiger-stripe pattern on leaves (interveinal chlorosis and necrosis). Berries develop dark spots. Internal wood shows brown streaking.
cure: Remove and destroy infected wood. Protect pruning wounds with fungicide paste. No complete cure exists once established.
prevention: Prune during dry weather. Apply wound protectants immediately after pruning. Avoid large pruning cuts.

name: Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spot)
cause: Caused by the fungus Pseudocercospora vitis. Favored by warm, humid conditions.
symptoms: Irregular dark brown spots on upper leaf surface. Grayish sporulation on lower leaf surface. Severe infections cause defoliation.
cure: Apply fungicides and remove infected leaves. Improve vineyard sanitation.
prevention: Manage vineyard hygiene, ensure good air circulation, and avoid overhead irrigation.

name: Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening)
cause: Caused by the bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus. Spread by the Asian citrus psyllid insect.
symptoms: Asymmetric yellowing (blotchy mottle) of leaves. Small, lopsided, bitter fruit. Premature fruit drop. Twig dieback.
cure: No cure exists. Infected trees must be removed and destroyed. Control psyllid populations with insecticides.
prevention: Use certified disease-free nursery stock. Monitor and control psyllid populations. Quarantine infected areas.

name: Peach___Bacterial_spot
cause: Caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas campestris pv. pruni. Spreads through rain splash and wind.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn purple-brown with yellow halos. Fruit develops sunken, dark lesions. Twig cankers.
cure: Apply copper-based bactericides during the growing season. Remove infected twigs during dormant pruning.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation. Apply copper sprays preventively in spring.

cure: Apply copper-based bactericides. Remove and destroy infected plant material. Avoid working in wet fields.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed. Rotate crops. Avoid overhead irrigation. Plant resistant varieties.

name: Potato___Early_blight
cause: Caused by the fungus Alternaria solani. Favored by warm temperatures and alternating wet and dry periods.
symptoms: Dark brown to black lesions with concentric rings (target-board pattern) on older leaves. Yellow halo around lesions. Premature defoliation.
cure: Apply fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb) at first sign of disease. Remove infected lower leaves.
prevention: Crop rotation, proper plant spacing, and avoiding overhead irrigation. Use certified seed potatoes.

name: Potato___Late_blight
cause: Caused by Phytophthora infestans. Spreads rapidly in cool, wet conditions. Responsible for the Irish Potato Famine.
symptoms: Water-soaked, pale green to brown lesions on leaves with white mold on undersides. Dark brown lesions on stems. Tubers show reddish-brown rot.
cure: Apply fungicides (metalaxyl, chlorothalonil) preventively and at first sign. Destroy infected plants immediately.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed. Plant resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation. Monitor weather forecasts.

name: Squash___Powdery_mildew
cause: Caused by fungal pathogens including Erysiphe cichoracearum and Sphaerotheca fuliginea. Thrives in warm, dry conditions.
symptoms: White to gray powdery coating on leaf surfaces and stems. Infected leaves turn yellow and die. Reduced fruit quality.
cure: Apply sulfur-based fungicides, neem oil, or potassium bicarbonate. Remove heavily infected leaves.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties. Ensure good air circulation. Avoid overhead watering.

name: Strawberry___Leaf_scorch
cause: Caused by the fungus Diplocarpon earlianum. Spreads through rain splash in warm, wet conditions.
symptoms: Small, irregular purple to dark brown spots on upper leaf surface. Centers turn tan to gray. Severe infections cause leaf scorch and defoliation.
cure: Remove and destroy infected leaves. Apply fungicides (captan, myclobutanil) during the growing season.
prevention: Avoid overhead irrigation. Renovate beds after harvest. Plant resistant varieties.

name: Tomato___Bacterial_spot
cause: Caused by Xanthomonas spp. Spreads through rain splash, contaminated tools, and infected transplants.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn brown with yellow halos. Raised, scabby lesions on fruit. Defoliation in severe cases.
cure: Apply copper-based bactericides. Remove infected plant material. Avoid working in wet conditions.
prevention: Use certified disease-free transplants. Rotate crops. Avoid overhead irrigation.

name: Tomato___Early_blight
cause: Caused by the fungus Alternaria solani. Favored by warm temperatures and wet conditions.
symptoms: Dark brown lesions with concentric rings (target-board pattern) on older leaves. Yellow halo around lesions. Stem lesions near soil line.
cure: Apply fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb). Remove infected lower leaves. Stake plants to improve airflow.
prevention: Crop rotation, mulching, and avoiding overhead irrigation. Remove plant debris after harvest.

name: Tomato___Late_blight
cause: Caused by Phytophthora infestans. Spreads rapidly in cool, wet conditions.
symptoms: Large, irregular, water-soaked lesions on leaves that turn brown. White mold on leaf undersides. Dark brown lesions on stems and fruit.
cure: Apply fungicides (metalaxyl, chlorothalonil) preventively. Destroy infected plants immediately to prevent spread.
prevention: Use resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation. Monitor weather and apply preventive fungicides.

name: Tomato___Leaf_Mold
cause: Caused by the fungus Passalora fulva (formerly Cladosporium fulvum). Thrives in high humidity environments.
symptoms: Pale green to yellow spots on upper leaf surface. Olive-green to brown velvety mold on lower leaf surface. Infected leaves curl and drop.
cure: Apply fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb). Improve greenhouse ventilation. Remove infected leaves.
prevention: Reduce humidity below 85%. Ensure good air circulation. Use resistant varieties.

name: Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot
cause: Caused by the fungus Septoria lycopersici. Spreads through rain splash and infected plant debris.
symptoms: Numerous small, circular spots with dark brown borders and gray-white centers on lower leaves. Tiny black dots (pycnidia) visible in spot centers.
cure: Apply fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb). Remove infected lower leaves. Avoid overhead watering.
prevention: Crop rotation, mulching, and removing plant debris. Stake plants to improve airflow.

name: Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider_mite
cause: Infestation by Tetranychus urticae (two-spotted spider mite). Thrives in hot, dry conditions. Populations explode rapidly.
symptoms: Fine stippling (tiny yellow dots) on upper leaf surface. Bronze or silvery discoloration. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaf drop in severe cases.
cure: Apply miticides or insecticidal soaps. Introduce predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis). Increase humidity.
prevention: Avoid water stress. Monitor plants regularly. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill natural predators.

name: Tomato___Target_Spot
cause: Caused by the fungus Corynespora cassiicola. Favored by warm, humid conditions.
symptoms: Brown lesions with concentric rings (target pattern) on leaves. Lesions may have yellow halos. Fruit develops sunken, dark lesions.
cure: Apply fungicides (chlorothalonil, azoxystrobin). Remove infected leaves and improve air circulation.
prevention: Crop rotation, proper plant spacing, and avoiding overhead irrigation.

name: Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus
cause: Caused by Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV). Transmitted by the silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci).
symptoms: Upward curling and yellowing of young leaves. Stunted plant growth. Reduced fruit set. Flowers may drop.
cure: No cure for infected plants. Remove and destroy infected plants. Control whitefly populations with insecticides or reflective mulches.
prevention: Use resistant varieties. Install insect-proof screens. Use yellow sticky traps to monitor whiteflies.

name: Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus
cause: Caused by Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV). Transmitted through contact, contaminated tools, and infected seed.
symptoms: Mosaic pattern of light and dark green on leaves. Leaf distortion and curling. Stunted growth. Fruit may show internal browning.
cure: No cure. Remove and destroy infected plants. Sterilize all tools with bleach solution.
prevention: Use certified virus-free seed. Wash hands before handling plants. Sterilize tools between plants. Plant resistant varieties.
